chapters.title: 1.1 Databases, Tables, Rows, Columns, Schemas
chapters.overviewText: A database server (one running MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQL Server) hosts one or more databases. A database contains tables, plus other objects like views and indexes. A table has columns (the structure) and rows (the data). Most people picture this as a nested set of containers: Server (MySQL instance on qa-db:3306) └── Database: hrms_qa ├── Table: employees → columns: employee_id, first_name, email, ... ├── Table: leave_requests → columns: leave_request_id, employee_id, status, ...

- Hierarchy: server → database → (schema) → table → columns/rows.
- "Schema" = the structure overall, and also a namespace in PostgreSQL (public) and SQL Server (dbo). In MySQL, schema = database.
- Row = one record, column = one attribute, cell may be NULL.
- Not a spreadsheet: enforced types, no guaranteed row order, rows identified by primary key.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Data is organized in a hierarchy
A database server (one running MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQL Server) hosts one or more databases. A database contains tables, plus other objects like views and indexes. A table has columns (the structure) and rows (the data). Most people picture this as a nested set of containers:
Server (MySQL instance on qa-db:3306)
 └── Database: hrms_qa
## └── Schema: (see below)
           ├── Table: employees      → columns: employee_id, first_name, email, ...
           ├── Table: leave_requests → columns: leave_request_id, employee_id, status, ...
## └── Table: payroll

When a tester says "check the DB," they usually mean "connect to this server, pick this database, and query these tables." Knowing which level you're at prevents the classic mistake of running a query against the wrong database, or the right database on the wrong server (say staging instead of QA).
## What "schema" means (and why it confuses everyone)
The word has two related meanings. In everyday conversation, "the schema" means the structure of the database: which tables exist, their columns, types and constraints. In SQL Server and PostgreSQL, a schema is also a specific namespace inside a database that groups tables. PostgreSQL's default is public, SQL Server's is dbo. In MySQL, "schema" and "database" are just synonyms for the same thing.

| MySQL | PostgreSQL | SQL Server | Hierarchy | Server → Database (= schema) → Table |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Server → Database → Schema → Table | Server → Database → Schema → Table | Default schema | The database itself | public |
| dbo | Fully qualified name | hrms_qa.employees | hrms_qa.public.employees (or public.employees) | hrms_qa.dbo.employees |

The fully qualified name matters when a query touches two databases or when your client's active database isn't the one you thought. SELECT * FROM hrms_qa.employees; works in MySQL no matter which database you're currently "in."
## Tables, rows and columns
A table models one kind of thing (employees, leave requests, payroll runs). A column is one attribute of that thing, and it has a fixed name and data type. A row (also called a record or tuple) is one specific instance. A single intersection of a row and a column is a cell or field value. A cell can also hold NULL, meaning "no value / unknown," which is different from zero or an empty string (Chapter 2.3 is dedicated to it).
## A table is not a spreadsheet
## The spreadsheet picture helps at first, but a few differences matter for testing:
Every column has an enforced type. You can't put "abc" in a date column.
Rows have no guaranteed order. Without ORDER BY, the database may return rows in any order, and that order can change between runs. Never write a test that assumes "the first row returned is the newest." This is the SQL cousin of a flaky test that depends on DOM order that isn't guaranteed.
Rows are identified by keys, not by position. There's no "row 7." There is employee_id = 7.
No merged cells, no formulas in cells. Calculated values are either computed at query time or stored as plain values (like net_pay), which is exactly why we verify stored calculations in Part 6.
## Primary keys, briefly
Almost every table has a primary key, a column (or combination of columns) whose value uniquely identifies each row, such as employee_id. It can't be NULL and can't repeat. Foreign keys (like employees.department_id) point to primary keys in other tables. We treat keys formally in 8.1, and use them for joins in Part 4. For now, just know that "one row = one primary key value."
Exploring what's in a database
Before you can query anything, you need to know what exists:
```sql
-- MySQL
```
| SHOW DATABASES;              -- list databases on the server | USE hrms_practice;           -- switch to one |
|---|---|
| SHOW TABLES;                 -- list tables | DESCRIBE employees;          -- columns, types, nullability, keys |

```sql
-- PostgreSQL (psql shell)
```
| \l                 -- list databases | \c hrms_practice   -- connect to one |
|---|---|
| \dt                -- list tables | \d employees       -- describe a table |

-- Works on all three via the standard information schema
```sql
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable
FROM   information_schema.columns
WHERE  table_name = 'employees';
```

information_schema is a set of built-in views that describe the database itself. GUI tools (DBeaver, Workbench, pgAdmin) show the same information in a tree. Chapter 8.6 builds a whole workflow on exploring an unfamiliar database; for now, get used to typing DESCRIBE on any table before you query it.
## Naming conventions and case sensitivity
Most teams use snake_case names, and tables are named as plural nouns (employees, leave_requests). Don't assume, though. A legacy database might have tblEmp or EMPLOYEE_MASTER. Case handling differs by dialect. MySQL table names are case-sensitive on Linux servers but not on Windows, which produces the fun bug where a query works on a developer's laptop and fails on the QA server. PostgreSQL folds unquoted names to lowercase, so SELECT * FROM Employees finds employees, but a table created as "Employees" (quoted) needs the quotes forever.
## The tester's mapping from UI to tables
A useful mental exercise: for every screen in the app, ask which table(s) it reads from and which columns each field maps to. The "Employee List" screen reads employees (joined with departments for the department name). The "Add Employee" form writes one row to employees. The "Leave Balance" widget probably derives its number from leave_types and leave_requests. Once you can map UI to tables, you can predict where a bug will show up in the data. Selenium and Playwright locate elements in the DOM, which is a tree. SQL locates data in tables, which is a set of rows. Both are "find the thing you care about, then assert on it."

chapters.title: 1.2 Data Types
chapters.overviewText: A data type tells the database how to store a value, what operations are legal, and which values are rejected. Choosing the wrong type is a common source of subtle bugs (rounding errors, truncated text, wrong sort order), so testers benefit from reading a table's types before designing tests. The four main families are numeric, text, date/time, and "other" (boolean, enum, JSON, binary). Numeric types: integers Integer types differ by range: Boundary testing applies directly here. A column defined as TINYINT that's meant to hold "days of leave" will break at 128. An INT primary key on a high-volume table can overflow after about 2.1 billion inserts, a rare but famous production failure.

chapters.customSummary:
- Integers: mind the ranges (TINYINT, INT ≈ 2.1 billion, BIGINT).
- Money must be DECIMAL, never FLOAT/DOUBLE (0.1 + 0.2 problem).
- VARCHAR(n) length is a testable boundary; strict mode errors, non-strict silently truncates. Check charset (utf8mb4) for non-English text.
- Date/time: DATE vs DATETIME/TIMESTAMP; time zones and UTC storage cause "wrong time" false alarms and real bugs. Use ISO date literals.
- Others: boolean (TINYINT(1)/BIT), ENUM (every value is a test case), JSON, UUID.
- Gotchas: numbers stored as text sort alphabetically; implicit conversion ('abc' = 0 is true in MySQL).
- Turn each column definition into boundary tests, and compare UI limits (maxlength) with DB limits.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Every column declares what kind of value it holds
A data type tells the database how to store a value, what operations are legal, and which values are rejected. Choosing the wrong type is a common source of subtle bugs (rounding errors, truncated text, wrong sort order), so testers benefit from reading a table's types before designing tests. The four main families are numeric, text, date/time, and "other" (boolean, enum, JSON, binary).
Numeric types: integers
Integer types differ by range:

| Type | Typical range (signed) | Common use | TINYINT (MySQL, SQL Server 0–255) | -128 to 127 (MySQL) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flags, small counters | SMALLINT | -32,768 to 32,767 | Small codes | INT / INTEGER |
| ±2,147,483,647 (about 2.1 billion) | IDs, counts | BIGINT | ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ | Huge tables, event logs |

Boundary testing applies directly here. A column defined as TINYINT that's meant to hold "days of leave" will break at 128. An INT primary key on a high-volume table can overflow after about 2.1 billion inserts, a rare but famous production failure.
## Numeric types: decimals vs floats (the money rule)
DECIMAL(p, s) (also called NUMERIC) stores exact numbers: p is the total number of digits (precision), s the digits after the decimal point (scale). DECIMAL(10,2) holds values up to 99,999,999.99 with exactly two decimal places. FLOAT and DOUBLE store approximate binary values, which are faster but can't represent many decimal fractions exactly.
Any JavaScript tester already knows the symptom:
0.1 + 0.2   // 0.30000000000000004

The same thing can happen when floats are used in a database and summed. That is why payroll, invoices, deductions and appointment prices must use DECIMAL. When you're reviewing a schema and see salary DOUBLE, log a finding. When comparing computed amounts, test with values like 0.1, 0.01 and 999,999.99, and check rounding rules (ROUND is covered in 2.4).
Text types

| Type | Meaning | Notes | CHAR(n) | Fixed length, padded with spaces | Codes like country NP, IN |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| VARCHAR(n) | Variable length up to n characters | Names, emails, most text | TEXT | Long free text | Comments, descriptions; often can't be fully indexed |

The n in VARCHAR(50) is a boundary a tester can attack: does the UI allow 51 characters while the column only accepts 50? In MySQL's default strict mode you get an error ("Data too long for column"); in a non-strict configuration the value is silently truncated, which is worse because no one notices. Also check character sets and collation: names in Devanagari, accented letters or emoji need utf8mb4 in MySQL. A column stuck on an older charset shows ???? for those characters. Collation also decides whether comparisons are case-sensitive (Chapter 2.5).
Date and time types

| Concept | MySQL | PostgreSQL | SQL Server |
|---|---|---|---|
| Date only | DATE | DATE | DATE |
| Time only | TIME | TIME | TIME |
| Date + time | DATETIME, TIMESTAMP | TIMESTAMP, TIMESTAMPTZ | DATETIME2, DATETIMEOFFSET |

The tester-relevant question is time zones. MySQL's TIMESTAMP converts to and from UTC using the session time zone, while DATETIME stores exactly what you give it. PostgreSQL TIMESTAMPTZ stores an absolute instant. If your UI shows a check-in of 09:05 but the DB shows 03:20, that is not necessarily a bug. It may be UTC, and Nepal's offset is UTC+5:45, so the difference shows up as an odd half-hour value. Always find out how the app stores time. Attendance and appointment features are the most exposed to this, especially around midnight, where a date can shift by a day.
Always write date literals in ISO format 'YYYY-MM-DD' or 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'. Formats like '05/10/2026' are ambiguous (5 October or 10 May?) and dialect-dependent.
## Other types worth recognizing
Boolean: BOOLEAN in PostgreSQL; MySQL's BOOLEAN is just TINYINT(1) where 0 = false and 1 = true (so the value 2 can sneak in); SQL Server uses BIT. Our is_deleted flag is this.
ENUM: a column restricted to a fixed list (status ENUM('active','inactive','resigned')). MySQL has it natively, PostgreSQL uses CREATE TYPE ... AS ENUM, and SQL Server usually uses a CHECK constraint or a lookup table. Enum columns are gold for testers: every allowed value is a test case, and every disallowed value should be rejected.
JSON: JSON (MySQL), JSON/JSONB (PostgreSQL), text with JSON functions (SQL Server). Used for flexible settings or payloads.
UUID: globally unique IDs. UUID in PostgreSQL, CHAR(36) or BINARY(16) in MySQL, UNIQUEIDENTIFIER in SQL Server.
BLOB / BYTEA / VARBINARY: binary files. Usually apps store files elsewhere and keep only a path in the DB.
## Type-related gotchas
Numbers stored as text sort alphabetically. If employee_code is VARCHAR, then '9' sorts after '10', because the comparison goes character by character.
Implicit conversion can hide bugs. MySQL will happily evaluate 'abc' = 0 as true (with a warning), and comparing a text column to a number forces conversion of every row, which can also defeat indexes. PostgreSQL is stricter and raises an error, which is safer. If you compare mismatched types and get surprising results, check the column type first.
Using types to design tests
Read the column definition and turn it into test data:

| Column definition | Test values to try | first_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL | 1 char, 50 chars, 51 chars, empty string, only spaces, emoji, Devanagari, NULL | days DECIMAL(4,1) | 0.5, 0.0, 999.9, 1000.0 (overflow), 0.55 (rounding) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| hire_date DATE | today, future date, 2026-02-29 (invalid), 1900-01-01 | status ENUM(...) | each valid value, an invalid value, wrong case | email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE | duplicates differing only in case or trailing space |

And to compare against what the UI enforces, ask the database directly:
```sql
SELECT column_name, data_type, character_maximum_length, is_nullable, column_default
FROM   information_schema.columns
WHERE  table_schema = 'hrms_practice'
  AND  table_name   = 'employees';
```

Then contrast with the UI. In Playwright, an input's maxlength attribute tells you what the front end allows:
```ts
const max = await page.getByLabel('First name').getAttribute('maxlength');
// UI says 100? DB says VARCHAR(50)? That mismatch is a bug waiting for a long name.
```

UI validation, API validation and DB constraints are three separate layers. A field that is limited only in the UI can still be pushed past the limit through the API, and the database is the last line of defence.

chapters.title: 1.3 SELECT, FROM, WHERE Basics
chapters.overviewText: SELECT says which columns you want, FROM says which table, and WHERE says which rows. Only the first two are required. Keywords aren't case-sensitive (select = SELECT), but the convention is uppercase keywords and lowercase names so queries are easy to read. Statements end with a semicolon, and whitespace and line breaks are ignored, so format for readability.

chapters.customSummary:
- SELECT reads, FROM names the table, WHERE filters rows; SELECT never modifies data.
- Use SELECT * to explore, name columns in tests and saved checks.
- Aliases with AS; expressions allowed in the select list.
- Single quotes for string/date values; double quotes are identifiers in PostgreSQL/SQL Server.
- Logical execution order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT (so aliases can't be used in WHERE).
- Analogy: FROM = which list, WHERE = locator filter, SELECT = which attributes to read, COUNT(*) = locator.count().
- Compare UI counts with DB counts, and apply the same business filters as the app (e.g., is_deleted = 0).
chapters.contentMarkdown:
```sql
SELECT retrieves data, and it never changes anything
SELECT is the most-used SQL statement and completely safe: it reads, never modifies. The minimal form is:
SELECT column1, column2
FROM   table_name
WHERE  condition;
```

SELECT says which columns you want, FROM says which table, and WHERE says which rows. Only the first two are required.
```sql
SELECT first_name, last_name, status
FROM   employees;
```

| first_name \| last_name \| status | Asha       \| Karki     \| active | Ravi       \| Shrestha  \| active |
|---|---|---|
| Mina       \| Thapa     \| active | Sita       \| Gurung    \| resigned | Bikash     \| Rai       \| inactive |

Keywords aren't case-sensitive (select = SELECT), but the convention is uppercase keywords and lowercase names so queries are easy to read. Statements end with a semicolon, and whitespace and line breaks are ignored, so format for readability.
```sql
SELECT * is convenient for looking, risky for tests
SELECT * returns every column:
SELECT * FROM employees;
```

It's perfect for exploring a table you've just met. It's a bad habit inside automated tests and saved sanity checks, because adding or reordering a column in the table changes what your test gets back, and you may fetch sensitive columns (salary, IDs) you never needed. In tests, name your columns. Also on large production-like tables, SELECT * without a filter can pull millions of rows, so add LIMIT (2.2) while exploring.
## Choosing columns, aliases and expressions
You can rename output columns with AS and compute new values right in the SELECT list:
```sql
SELECT employee_id                        AS id,
       CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) AS full_name,
       email
FROM   employees;
```

| id \| full_name       \| email | 1  \| Asha Karki      \| asha@example.com |
|---|---|
| 2  \| Ravi Shrestha   \| ravi@example.com | ... |

Arithmetic works too: SELECT basic_salary + allowances - deductions AS expected_net FROM payroll;. Expressions and functions get their own chapter (2.4). You can even SELECT 1 + 1; without a FROM clause, handy as a "is my connection alive?" check.
WHERE filters rows
WHERE keeps only rows for which the condition is true:
```sql
SELECT employee_id, first_name, status
FROM   employees
WHERE  status = 'active';
```

| employee_id \| first_name \| status | 1           \| Asha       \| active |
|---|---|
| 2           \| Ravi       \| active | 3           \| Mina       \| active |

Strings and dates go in single quotes; numbers don't. A very common trap: double quotes mean identifiers (column/table names) in PostgreSQL and SQL Server, but MySQL by default treats double quotes as strings. To stay portable, always use single quotes for values.
## How the database reads your query
You write SELECT first, but the engine logically processes clauses in a different order:
1. FROM      → which table(s)
| 2. WHERE     → filter rows | 3. GROUP BY  → form groups           (Part 3) | 4. HAVING    → filter groups         (Part 3) |
|---|---|---|
| 5. SELECT    → pick/compute columns | 6. ORDER BY  → sort                  (2.2) | 7. LIMIT     → cut the result        (2.2) |

This explains an error that catches beginners. You can't use a SELECT alias inside WHERE, because WHERE runs before the alias exists:
-- Fails: 'id' doesn't exist yet when WHERE runs
```sql
SELECT employee_id AS id FROM employees WHERE id = 2;
```

-- Works: use the real column name
```sql
SELECT employee_id AS id FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 2;
```

The Selenium/Playwright analogy
If you already write locators, you already think this way:

| SQL | Test-automation equivalent | FROM employees | "Which list/page am I looking at?" | WHERE status = 'active' | rows.filter({ hasText: 'active' }) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SELECT first_name, email | Which attributes/text you read from the element | LIMIT 1 | .first() | COUNT(*) | await rows.count() |

That last one makes a powerful combined check: compare the number shown in the UI with the number in the database.
```ts
import mysql from 'mysql2/promise';
```

```ts
test('employee list count matches the database', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/employees?status=active');
  const uiCount = await page.locator('table#employees tbody tr').count();
```

| const db = await mysql.createConnection(process.env.QA_DB_URL!); | const [rows]: any = await db.execute( | 'SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM employees WHERE status = ? AND is_deleted = 0', |
|---|---|---|
| ['active'] | ); | await db.end(); |

  expect(uiCount).toBe(rows[0].total);   // 3 == 3
});

Notice the AND is_deleted = 0. The UI probably hides soft-deleted rows, so your query must apply the same rule the app applies. Getting the business filter right is half of DB testing. Soft deletes are covered in 8.4.
## Comments and readability
-- like this comments a single line (in MySQL, put a space after the two dashes), and /* ... */ comments a block. Comment your saved sanity-check queries with what they check and what a failing result means; future you (and your teammates) will be grateful.

| Common beginner errors | Error message (MySQL) | Usual cause | Unknown column 'Status' in 'field list' | Typo or wrong column name; check DESCRIBE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Table 'hrms.employee' doesn't exist | Wrong table name or wrong database selected | You have an error in your SQL syntax ... near ... | Missing comma/quote/keyword; look right at the spot the error names | Query returns 0 rows unexpectedly |

Appendix D collects these with fixes.

chapters.title: 1.4 Comparison & Logical Operators
chapters.overviewText: These compare a column to a value and produce true, false, or (with NULL) unknown: Use <> rather than != if you want strict standard SQL, though all three major databases accept both. A single = is used for comparison (not == as in JavaScript). LIKE patterns are covered fully in 2.5 and NULL in 2.3, but you need a taste of them now. Examples on our data: -- Employees hired in 2025 or later

chapters.customSummary:
- Comparison: =, <>/!=, <, >, <=, >=, BETWEEN (inclusive), IN, LIKE, IS NULL.
- Logical: AND, OR, NOT; precedence is NOT → AND → OR, so use parentheses when mixing.
- BETWEEN on DATETIME columns misses the last day; use >= start AND < next_start.
- > vs >= is where off-by-one bugs live; test boundaries on both sides.
- NOT IN and = NULL behave unexpectedly with NULL (see 2.3).
- Query-for-violations pattern: select the bad rows; zero rows = pass. Maps to expect(rows).toHaveLength(0) and is the backbone of Parts 6 and 10.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Comparison operators
These compare a column to a value and produce true, false, or (with NULL) unknown:

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| = | equal | status = 'active' |
| <> or != | not equal | status <> 'resigned' |
| < > | less / greater than | hire_date > '2025-01-01' |
| <= >= | less-or-equal / greater-or-equal | days >= 3 |
| BETWEEN a AND b | in range, inclusive of both ends | days BETWEEN 1 AND 3 |
| IN (...) | matches any value in a list | status IN ('pending','approved') |
| LIKE | pattern match | email LIKE '%@example.com' |
| IS NULL / IS NOT NULL | tests for missing value | manager_id IS NULL |

Use <> rather than != if you want strict standard SQL, though all three major databases accept both. A single = is used for comparison (not == as in JavaScript). LIKE patterns are covered fully in 2.5 and NULL in 2.3, but you need a taste of them now.
Examples on our data:
-- Employees hired in 2025 or later
```sql
SELECT first_name, hire_date FROM employees WHERE hire_date >= '2025-01-01';
```

first_name | hire_date
Ravi       | 2025-03-10
Bikash     | 2025-09-01

-- Leave requests still needing action
```sql
SELECT leave_request_id, employee_id, status
FROM   leave_requests
WHERE  status IN ('pending');
```

IN shines when the list grows: WHERE status IN ('pending','approved','rejected') is far cleaner than three OR conditions.
## Logical operators: AND, OR, NOT
AND requires both conditions, OR requires at least one, and NOT reverses a condition:
-- Active QA staff who are not soft-deleted
```sql
SELECT first_name, last_name
```
| FROM   employees | WHERE  department_id = 2 |
|---|---|
| AND  status = 'active' | AND  is_deleted = 0; |

first_name | last_name
Asha       | Karki
## Ravi       | Shrestha

Bikash is in QA but excluded by two of the conditions (inactive and is_deleted = 1), which shows how each AND narrows the result.
## Precedence: the source of quiet bugs
NOT is evaluated first, then AND, then OR. That means these two queries are not the same:
-- Intended: pending OR approved leave, but only for employee 2
```sql
SELECT * FROM leave_requests
WHERE status = 'pending' OR status = 'approved' AND employee_id = 2;
-- Real meaning: (status = 'pending') OR (status = 'approved' AND employee_id = 2)
-- Returns ALL pending requests (employee 3's too), which is wrong.
```

```sql
SELECT * FROM leave_requests
WHERE (status = 'pending' OR status = 'approved') AND employee_id = 2;
-- Correct
```

Rule of thumb: whenever you mix AND and OR, add parentheses. It costs nothing and removes ambiguity. This bug is especially nasty in test queries, because it usually returns some plausible rows, so you don't notice you're checking the wrong set.
NOT and negation
```sql
SELECT first_name FROM employees WHERE NOT status = 'resigned';   -- same as status <> 'resigned'
SELECT first_name FROM employees WHERE status NOT IN ('resigned','inactive');
SELECT first_name FROM employees WHERE email NOT LIKE '%@example.com';
```

Careful with NOT IN when the list or column contains NULL. The result can be empty for a surprising reason. That trap is explained in 2.3 and again with subqueries in 5.1.
## BETWEEN and date ranges: the classic off-by-one
BETWEEN includes both endpoints: days BETWEEN 1 AND 3 matches 1, 2 and 3. That is fine for numbers and DATE columns. With DATETIME/TIMESTAMP columns it hides a bug:
-- Meant: everything created in September 2026
```sql
SELECT * FROM leave_requests
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-09-01' AND '2026-09-30';
```

'2026-09-30' is interpreted as 2026-09-30 00:00:00, so anything created during 30 September after midnight is missed. The safe pattern is a half-open range:
```sql
SELECT * FROM leave_requests
WHERE created_at >= '2026-09-01'
  AND created_at <  '2026-10-01';
```

```sql
Use this whenever the column includes a time part. It also mirrors how the app itself should filter, so if a "This Month" report is missing last-day records, this is a prime suspect. Reports and dashboards are validated in 9.6.
```
## Operators as boundary-testing tools
The difference between > and >= is the difference between a working feature and an off-by-one defect. When a business rule says "employees with 5 or more sick days must submit a certificate," write the query both ways and check the app agrees with the correct version:
```sql
SELECT employee_id, SUM(days) AS sick_days   -- SUM is introduced in Part 3
FROM   leave_requests
WHERE  leave_type_id = 2 AND status = 'approved'
GROUP  BY employee_id
HAVING SUM(days) >= 5;   -- boundary: exactly 5 must be included
```

Then test the app with 4, 5 and 6 days.
## The "query for violations" pattern
This is the most important idea in the whole chapter for a QA engineer. Instead of writing a query that returns good data and eyeballing it, write a query that returns bad data. An empty result means the check passes; any rows returned are bugs.
-- Approved leave with no approver recorded
```sql
SELECT leave_request_id, employee_id
FROM   leave_requests
WHERE  status = 'approved' AND approved_by IS NULL;
```

-- Leave that ends before it starts
```sql
SELECT leave_request_id, start_date, end_date
FROM   leave_requests
WHERE  end_date < start_date;
```

-- Resigned employees still marked as not deleted and hired in the future (impossible dates)
```sql
SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE hire_date > CURRENT_DATE;
```

In Playwright or pytest this maps straight onto an assertion: run the query and expect(rows).toHaveLength(0). Part 6 turns this pattern into a systematic validation approach, and Part 10 builds a reusable library of these checks for attendance, payroll, appointments and leave.
## Truth values in short
Every condition evaluates to TRUE, FALSE or, when NULL is involved, UNKNOWN. WHERE keeps only rows where the whole condition is TRUE, so a row where the condition is UNKNOWN is silently dropped. That is why WHERE manager_id = NULL returns nothing (it should be IS NULL), and why WHERE manager_id <> 1 doesn't return employees with no manager. Chapter 2.3 covers this fully.
